newsitem.title: UK: EC queries Esso in UK licensees' protest.
newsitem.headline: EC queries Esso in UK licensees' protest.

text.p: The European Commission has requested information from Esso Petroleum regarding a complaint lodged by its own petrol retail license holders in Great Britain in the wake of last year's Pricewatch campaign, an Esso spokeswoman told Reuters on Monday.

A spokesman for the Federation of Small Businesses in the U.K., which guided the 397 petrol stations in filing the complaint in January, said they now spoke for more than 600 of Esso's nearly 2,000 U.K. outlets.

Individual operators formed ELRA, or the Esso Licensees Retailers Association, to convince Brussels to investigate and force Esso to provide "commercial and financial benefits" in their licensee agreements, said Paul Horan, spokesman for both ELRA and the federation.

ELRA has also contacted Esso retailers in Germany, planned a national conference, and are banking on new 15-year EC regulations on petrol supply that are soon to expire to take into account its complaint, he said.

Esso, a unit of U.S. oil giant Exxon Corp, launched its Pricewatch campaign in early 1996 promising to match its lowest-priced competitors in a move that helped squeeze retail margins to break-even levels last summer.
"Certainly we had the European Commission contact us and asked us to provide them with some information," the Esso spokeswoman said. "We're in the process of responding."
Esso, the largest petrol retailer in the U.K. and displaying its brand at roughly 10,000 stations in Europe, said earlier this year that its U.K. retail earnings in 1996 were hurt by Pricewatch.

Low-cost hypermarkets and chronic overcapacity in the U.K., in addition to Pricewatch, led to a near 10 percent reduction in the number of stations last year, closing down nearly 1,500, industry analysts said.

Horan said the Esso licensees objected to what they said were an increase in site rental fees and reduced margins that were implemented by the oil giant to pay for its marketing campaign, which continues to this day.
Licensees can only make 0.75 pence per litre on the petrol it sells, he said, versus 1.25 pence prior to Pricewatch and a European average of seven pence.

"The licensee retailer feels like he is in a commercial straightjacket and is finding it difficult to compete," Horan said. "It's a Catch-22 because motorists are coming to his petrol site, and they might get cheaper petrol but he has to charge full price in the shop, so sales in the shop are being reduced."

ELRA, which unsuccessfully filed a complained with U.K. regulator the Office of Fair Trading, is still pursuing a conciliation procedure in their licenses and is additionally working to resolve the complaint directly with Esso.
Article 85 under the Treaty of Rome was specifically cited by Horan for the retailers to receive special commercial and financial advantage in their agreements with Esso.

"The licensees feel very insecure under the terms of the contract. However, that feeling of insecurity wasn't really apparent up to about 18 months ago when they started Pricewatch," he said. He added, "It's one of the biggest companies in the world and it now has the indignity of a complaint lodged against it."
